title: A Veteran Photographer Retires
body_markdown:
Sara Krulwich, the only journalist ever awarded a Tony, is retiring after 47 years. Read more from director of photography, Meaghan Looram, and photo editor, Becky Lebowitz.


Photo Credit: Todd Heisler /The New York Times


Sara Krulwich is retiring after more than 47 years as a staff photographer at The Times. During her career, she paved the way for women and gay journalists, created the culture photographer beat and remains the only journalist ever awarded a Tony.


Sara grew up in New York City and attended the University of Michigan, where she was the first woman photographer for The Michigan Daily in her freshman year. That year, football game press passes read, “No women, children or dogs allowed on the field.” Assigned to cover the first game of her sophomore year, security guards ordered her off the field. In front of more than 100,000 fans, she defied them and remained on the sidelines to photograph the game. It was her 19th birthday.


After graduating, Sara visited more than two dozen newspapers in search of a job. Male photo editors were largely uninterested in hiring a woman news photographer; one compared hiring a woman to hiring “half a person.” She went on to work at The Providence Journal, The Journal Inquirer and The Philadelphia Inquirer. In 1978, The Times settled a landmark class-action sex discrimination lawsuit brought by Betsy Wade on behalf of the newspaper’s female employees. And in 1979, Sara was among the women journalists hired in the wake of that settlement.


In her first 15 years at The Times, Sara covered everything from boxing at Madison Square Garden and the New York City Marathon crossing the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge to Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parades and Westminster Kennel Club Dog Shows. She photographed the 1984 presidential campaign and the AIDS crisis, as well as Alan Greenspan at his breakfast table, Manny Ramirez playing high school baseball and Ivana Trump at a hair salon.


In the early 1990s, Sara pitched a new beat to The Times: culture desk photographer. At the time, newspapers typically ran handout photos with theater stories. She wanted to apply the same journalistic rigor The Times applied to other subjects to theater photography.


Her longevity on the beat allowed her to build sources and an encyclopedic body of work. A few years ago, we found in her negatives a photo of a young Kelli O’Hara at a costume fitting before her first Broadway show as a company member, in 2001. When Sara photographed O’Hara again later that week, she brought the old image to show her. O’Hara teared up. In the 23 years since that fitting, she had earned nine Tony nominations and one award. Sara photographed every one of those shows.


“Theatergoers have a habit of writing critics to ask, with annoyance, ‘Did we even see the same show?’” said former Times chief theater critic Ben Brantley. “Looking at a Krulwich shot, I not only felt we’d seen the same show, I often felt that I was seeing it, in the flesh, all over again.”


In 2018, Sara became the first and only journalist to be recognized with a Tony Honor for Excellence in the Theater. She walked the red carpet as an honoree, then slid into her usual assigned location to cover the show.


Sara is known for that unfailing professionalism and just as much for her kindness. A treasured colleague and friend to so many, she is warm, supportive, funny and welcoming.


The newsroom Sara joined in 1979 had a long way to go. Female photographers didn’t get the same opportunities or even equipment as others. The Times would not print the word “gay” until a ban on that word was reversed in 1986. Change came slowly, and all the while, Sara helped create a safe, welcoming space for fellow women and gay colleagues at The Times.


— Meaghan & Becky


Photo Credit: Todd Heisler /The New York Times
